processing: A small version of the Qian Liang method: steamed Anhua raw dark tea is packed into a bamboo, leaf and smartweed wrap and tightened by hand, then cured in the air.
harvest_season: One maker's lot is listed as spring tea, but as with other Anhua rolls the pressing year counts for more than the picking.
appearance_dry: A short, tight, bamboo-wrapped roll of dark compressed tea.
appearance_liquor: Orange-yellow to orange-red and clear, deeper with age.
taste_profile: One aged lot is described as spicy, sweet and thick, with hints of brewer's yeast and mushroom. Light pine notes are typical of Anhua rolls.

brewing.notes: Take off the bamboo and saw or chip off a piece; one seller suggests a thin-kerf miter saw. Rinse once and use boiling water.

vintage_note: Sold whole by pressing year, and some shops sell small samples. Aged lots of about ten years or more are on the market alongside new ones. Stored dry and aired it keeps on changing, so a roll is often bought to drink over years.
description:
Shi Liang Cha is the small end of Anhua's rolled tea family: ten taels of dark tea in a bamboo wrap, a far more practical thing to own than a 36 kg column. One retailer lists it at 365 g, and the size may vary by maker.

It is made the way the bigger rolls are, with steamed raw tea packed into bamboo, leaf and smartweed and tightened by hand. A Hunan press account mentions more than twenty steps in making it.

A retailer's notes on one aged lot mention spice, sweetness and thick texture with yeast and mushroom, and that fits what you expect from an aged Anhua roll. The tea is hard, so break it into small chips, let them rest a few days and brew with boiling water.

Check the maker and year, and make sure the bamboo is sound and the smell clean. It is the easiest way to try the whole Qian Liang idea without a saw big enough for a tree trunk.
history:
Little is documented about Shi Liang's own beginnings. It belongs to the Hua Juan family, now usually called Anhua Qian Liang, whose largest size is dated by Hunan press accounts to the Jiaqing and Daoguang years.

The small roll looks like a modern convenience, but no firm date for its first production is recorded. Baishaxi, founded in 1939, is the factory most associated with the family's revival.
